prosaic

proh-ZAY-ik · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Prosaic is lacking poetic beauty or excitement; dull, ordinary, matter-of-fact.

Compared to the fantasy novel's soaring battle scenes, the sequel's prosaic account of tax paperwork felt like a letdown.

Worked Example

The travel brochure promised adventure, but the trip turned out to be a prosaic string of delayed buses and forgettable meals.

Prosaic describes something plain and unremarkable -- the opposite of vivid or inspired -- like everyday prose next to soaring poetry.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

mundane: Mundane (a word you met earlier in this course) points at the ordinary, everyday side of life — errands, laundry, paperwork. Prosaic judges the telling rather than the subject: a prosaic sentence can make even a shipwreck sound flat.

humdrum: Humdrum is dullness that comes from sameness — the same route, the same tasks, week after week. Prosaic can strike in a single flat sentence, but humdrum needs a routine that repeats.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

poetic: having the beauty or expressiveness of poetry

vivid: producing powerful, striking images

Where it sits · how dull and unoriginal it is — plain → prosaic → banal

plain vs. prosaic: Plain describes something simple, not especially exciting or beautiful, milder than prosaic.

banal vs. prosaic: Banal (a word you met earlier in this course) is so dull it's almost offensively unoriginal, even more extreme than prosaic.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — prose

root — prose: ordinary written or spoken language, without poetic structure (Latin prosa (oratio), 'straightforward (speech)')

suffix — -aic

suffix — -aic: having the qualities of (Greek/Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Prosaic comes directly from prose, ordinary written or spoken language without poetic rhythm or imagery. Something prosaic reads or feels like plain prose next to poetry -- flat and unremarkable.

Use the root in a new word: prose

Use the root in a new word: prose: Most novels are written in prose, while few modern writers still compose entire books in verse.
